rationale: The MIT notes use the same globally convergent factorial power series for exp, and Lebl defines e=exp(1). The library packages those two standard conventions in one definition and makes the canonical-natural embedding explicit, so the content is semantically standard but not verbatim from one source. A definition supplies no proof.

The MIT notes state that the exponential power series has infinite radius and hence converges for every real argument. The local proof replaces their ratio-test presentation by an explicit geometric-tail comparison.

Hunter Proposition 10.24 states E(x)E(y)=E(x+y) for all real x,y and proves it by the same Cauchy-product and binomial-theorem calculation. The library's embedded-factorial notation is only a notational convention.

Hunter states E(-x)=1/E(x) and E(x)>0 for every real x immediately after the addition formula; Johnson also derives reciprocal and positivity from the multiplicative equation. The local square argument is an adapted proof.

Hunter gives E'=E from the factorial series, while Lebl's analytic-functions section gives termwise derivatives and the resulting smoothness of power-series sums. The item combines these into the stronger all-orders identity exp^(m)=exp.

Lebl's exponential proposition states that exp is strictly increasing and differentiable with positive derivative. The local proof uses the mean value theorem rather than Lebl's inverse-log construction.

Lebl gives the limits 0 and +infinity at the two ends and range (0,infinity). The item restates these together with the elementary bound exp(x)>=1+x and a specific reciprocal proof; that proof is locally assembled.

Lebl states that the exponential is a strictly increasing bijection from R to (0,infinity), exactly the corollary's mathematical assertion. The library proof repackages monotonicity, endpoint limits, continuity, and IVT.

The MIT notes prove that the exponential dominates every fixed polynomial power using a retained factorial-series term. The item includes an arbitrary positive scaling a and spells out both infinity limits, a standard change of variables and reciprocal reformulation.
Hunter Proposition 10.25 and the Penn notes characterize exp as the unique differentiable solution of f'=f with f(0)=1. The local integrating-factor proof is a standard adaptation.

The Texas A&M notes give uniqueness of the continuous positive multiplicative function normalized at 1, and Johnson derives exponential form from continuity of a nonzero multiplicative solution. The item combines that standard characterization with the differentiability-at-zero normalization F(0)=F'(0)=1, so no one located source has its exact two-part packaging.

Princeton states for fixed k that binom(N,k)=N^k/k!(1+O(1/N)), which is semantically the exact asserted limit. Lebl and Hunter supply the surrounding product-limit and binomial context. The displayed finite-product proof and its additional bound in [0,1/k!] are local.

Lebl Exercise 5.4.5 states e^x=lim_n(1+x/n)^n for every real x, with the same eventual-domain convention implicit in a real sequence. The library supplies a binomial head-tail proof instead of Lebl's logarithmic hint.

Lebl's Picard example for y'=y, y(0)=1 gives the iterates 1+x+...+x^n/n! and their global limit exp. The item additionally records compact-uniform convergence and the limiting integral equation, so it is a faithful strengthened packaging; its induction and interchange proof adapt the standard construction.

The sources identify the ODE, factorial power series, product-limit, functional-equation, and Picard descriptions of the ordinary exponential across their sections. The item is a library-specific consolidation of five standard characterizations, and its proof is the local composition of the preceding equivalence results.

Both sources use the same factorial-tail domination needed in the classical irrationality proof. The item generalizes it to |x|<=1 and arbitrary cutoff N with the explicit factor 2, a routine geometric-tail estimate not located verbatim; the displayed derivation is local.

The LSU problem states 2<e<3 from the Taylor series and a geometric comparison, and the Michigan notes state and derive the same strict bounds. The local proof invokes the immediately preceding factorial-tail lemma.

Both university sources state that e is irrational and use the classical contradiction in which a factorial-scaled positive tail is an integer strictly between 0 and 1. The A8 repair preserves that classical argument while adding local typed derivations for positive denominators, factorial divisibility, and the nested embeddings into R, so the proof is now honestly classified as ai-altered.

This is a bespoke description of this repository's dependency order and explicitly names its own local theorem graph. Literature can support the mathematics it mentions but cannot contain this corpus-specific roadmap; it is therefore positively identified as locally invented. A remark of this kind supplies no proof.

This is a bespoke numerical specialization of the preceding all-real product-limit theorem at x=-2. Direct verification: substituting x=-2 gives the displayed limit exp(-2), and the addition and reciprocal laws give exp(-2)=1/(exp(1)exp(1))=e^-2>0. The two-step proof is likewise local.

This is a bespoke moving-point witness for failure of uniform convergence of the just-defined product-limit sequence. Direct verification: at x=n the nth function equals 2^n, whereas exp(n)=e^n and e>2, so the error (e^n-2^n) is unbounded. No located source contained this exact witness, and the construction is completely checked from stated dependencies.

Lebl and the MIT notes give the same one-sided function exp(-1/x) for x>0 and 0 for x<=0, state it is smooth, and state that all derivatives at 0 vanish. The local polynomial-times-exponential induction follows the standard proof with repository notation.

Dyatlov's MIT notes give exactly exp(-1/(1-|x|^2)) on the unit ball and zero outside as a C-infinity compactly supported bump; in one dimension this is the item's formula. The local proof phrases it as composition with the previously constructed flat function.

Johnson constructs discontinuous positive solutions of F(x+y)=F(x)F(y) using a Hamel-basis choice, and Gselmann records additive Hamel-basis extensions and exponential solutions exp(A(x)). The item's choice of one basis element b and values A(1)=1, A(b)=0 is a concrete adaptation of that standard construction.

The UTSA notes explicitly state that the real exponential is not uniformly continuous on the whole real line. The library proof uses the standard close-pairs criterion and the mean value theorem with x_n=n and y_n=n+1/n.
